Protect abortion access

sos-1601663.background: Incumbent King County Councilmember for District 8 since 2024, chair of the Health, Housing and Human Services Committee and the King County Board of Health, and a Sound Transit Board member. Previously served two terms on the Seattle City Council and worked at the Washington State Labor Council.

record.text: Sponsored a 2026 ordinance, approved by the council, restricting use of county-owned property as a staging area or operations base for civil immigration enforcement.
Sponsored a one-year emergency moratorium (2026), approved by the council, on accepting permits for new or expanded detention facilities in unincorporated King County.
Sponsored legislation (2025), passed unanimously, prohibiting large corporate landlords in unincorporated King County from using algorithmic rent-setting platforms.
Issued a statement supporting the June 2026 King County Transportation District action funding unincorporated roads, with a share for cities.
As a Sound Transit Board member, issued a statement supporting the May 2026 Sound Transit 20-year financial plan vote covering West Seattle Link and other ST3 projects.
On the Seattle City Council, led passage in 2020 of the JumpStart payroll expense tax on large employers (described on her campaign site as progressive revenue for housing and other investments).

sos-1601664.background: Former data analytics and technology consultant who most recently worked as a legislative assistant to Seattle City Councilmember Maritza Rivera. Has not held elected office, so has no voting record.

housing.summary: Both candidates say they want more housing built. Mosqueda emphasizes public and nonprofit funding (including a regional housing levy and progressive revenue) and sponsored a ban on algorithmic rent-setting; Duda emphasizes faster permitting, fewer development barriers and much more density near light rail, and says public budgets alone cannot close the gap. On homelessness, Mosqueda describes a housing-first approach with outcome benchmarks; Duda calls for leading with addiction treatment, sober housing and rebuilding the regional system around measurable goals.

build_more.why: Supports incentives and zoning to build more housing, including density near transit.

evidence.quote: Create incentives to build more green, lasting and affordable housing throughout our region in partnership with local jurisdictions and communities to promote density
leverage county financing, zoning, and surplus land policies to build more affordable units near transit and job centers

public_housing.why: Supports public and nonprofit housing funding, including social housing developers, land trusts and a regional housing levy.

evidence.quote: I support community land trusts and nonprofit social housing developers to take land permanently off the speculative market
I support the growing call for a regional Housing Levy to scale up housing in our region to meet the need.

tenant_protections.why: Sponsored a county ban on algorithmic rent-setting by large corporate landlords and lists preventing displacement as a priority.

evidence.quote: unanimously passed legislation sponsored by Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda to prohibit large corporate landlords from using algorithmic rent price fixing platforms
My priorities remain expanding affordable housing and preventing displacement

housing_first.why: Supports a housing-first approach and expanding permanent supportive housing with services.

evidence.quote: I support a housing-first, evidence-based approach with clear outcome benchmarks and rigorous fiscal oversight.
I will fight to expand permanent supportive housing and the workforce required to succeed

treatment.why: Supports investing in behavioral health services and workers.

evidence.quote: Increase access to care by investing in behavioral health services and workers

spending_accountability.why: Points to steps to bring homelessness contracts back under county oversight, including an independent financial monitor, and calls for outcome benchmarks and oversight hearings.

evidence.quote: we hired an independent financial monitor

My approach is to build accountability in from the start: clear outcome benchmarks, transparent reporting, timely payments to contracted providers, and regular oversight hearings so problems are caught early.

build_more.why: Supports fixing permitting and allowing much more housing near light rail stations.

evidence.quote: It means building more housing by fixing permitting and reducing barriers to new construction
Allow significantly more housing within several blocks of major light-rail stations

less_regulation_tax.why: Says development requirements and barriers make housing harder to finance and should be reduced to expand private supply.

evidence.quote: We need to greatly reduce barriers for private development to expand the total supply
Development requirements make projects difficult to finance, meaning less housing actually gets built.

public_housing.why: Supports public housing that is safe and stabilizing for the most vulnerable, while saying government cannot build its way out of the shortage alone.

evidence.quote: public housing that is safe and stabilizing for our most vulnerable
There is no municipal budget that won’t collapse if local government tries to build its way out of the gap.

treatment.why: Wants treatment as the primary response to addiction-related homelessness, with more public treatment beds, private beds when needed, and sober recovery housing.

evidence.quote: Contract with qualified private providers when public beds are unavailable.
Create dedicated sober housing throughout the county-funded housing system.
Housing matters, but for someone suffering from severe addiction, housing alone is not treatment.

enforce_encampments.why: Calls for clear expectations on public safety and public spaces alongside services.

evidence.quote: We need a much stronger treatment, recovery, and accountability framework that connects people to services, but also sets clear expectations around public safety and public spaces.

spending_accountability.why: Supports moving away from the current regional homelessness authority structure and measuring each program against clear goals.

evidence.quote: Yes, I support moving away from the current KCRHA structure.
Each program should have clear measurable goals and outcomes and should be regularly measured against them.

safety.summary: Both candidates mention violence prevention for young people. Mosqueda frames gun and youth violence as a public health issue and calls for prevention programs and for stronger follow-through on law enforcement oversight recommendations. Duda calls for recruiting and retaining officers, escalating consequences for repeat offenders, aggressive pursuit of traffickers and dealers, and fixing jail medical intake; he said he did not yet have a position on making oversight recommendations binding.

prevention.why: Supports gun and youth violence prevention programs and funding for community-based services.

evidence.quote: Address gun, youth, and interpersonal violence as the public health crisis they are by expanding gun awareness programming and money for dispute resolution programming
improving community safety through behavioral health and gun violence prevention

police_accountability.why: Says advisory-only oversight (OLEO) recommendations are insufficient and the council should push for stronger accountability on use of force and traffic enforcement.

evidence.quote: The current advisory-only structure for OLEO recommendations is insufficient
I believe the Council should be much more actively involved in advancing these recommendations, particularly around use of force, traffic enforcement, and community safety.

more_police.why: Supports competitive pay and staffing to recruit and retain officers.

evidence.quote: We should recruit, train, and retain excellent officers, compensate them competitively, and expect professionalism in return.

tougher_enforcement.why: Supports escalating consequences for repeat offenders after diversion and aggressively pursuing traffickers and drug dealers.

evidence.quote: Escalate consequences for repeated offenses when previous interventions have failed.
Aggressively pursue pimps, dealers, and organized exploitation.

prevention.why: Supports youth programs and earlier intervention in areas with persistent violence, and stabilization centers for people in crisis.

evidence.quote: Expand youth sports, mentorship, employment, and after-school opportunities in neighborhoods experiencing persistent violence.

police_accountability.why: Says independent oversight of law enforcement is essential, but said he needed more information before taking a position on binding OLEO recommendations.

evidence.quote: I am a firm believer in accountability and measurable outcomes, and believe independent oversight is essential to public trust, especially in law enforcement.

cost.summary: Mosqueda says she will pursue progressive revenue such as a progressive payroll tax and real estate excise tax, and opposes using accountability concerns to cut social services. Duda focuses on audits, outcome statements and withholding funds from programs that cannot define success and says better delivery can provide more effective services.

tax_wealthy.why: Supports progressive revenue, including a progressive payroll tax and progressive real estate excise tax; led Seattle's JumpStart payroll tax.

evidence.quote: I will pursue progressive revenue – including a progressive payroll tax and progressive REET
leading the passage of progressive revenue to invest in housing

cut_spending.why: Opposes using financial-mismanagement findings as a reason to cut social services, while supporting stronger controls.

evidence.quote: I refuse to let legitimate accountability concerns become a backdoor to austerity.

cut_spending.why: Supports stronger audits and outcome-based budgeting, including withholding part of a large program's funding until it sets measurable goals.

evidence.quote: Strengthen independent performance and financial audits.
25% of its funding should be withheld until it can.

transport.summary: Both candidates support frequent, reliable transit and protecting service. Mosqueda emphasizes building all ST3 light rail lines, around-the-clock service, new transit revenue, a road-funding district and bike and pedestrian safety. Duda emphasizes fare gates paired with reduced fares, reassessing project costs, exploring lower-cost rail alternatives, and denser housing around stations.

transit.why: Supports building all voter-approved ST3 lines and expanding frequent, around-the-clock transit service.

evidence.quote: expand frequent, reliable, electrified transit service around the clock
Abandonment is not an option – neither is indefinitely deferring lines King County riders are counting on.

roads.why: Supported a Transportation Benefit District to fund road repairs in unincorporated areas such as White Center and Vashon.

evidence.quote: Today’s action provides much needed relief for unincorporated roads, bike lanes and sidewalks to be built on the horizon.

safe_streets.why: Supports protected bike lanes and safe crossings.

evidence.quote: I've advocated to advance safe walking and biking infrastructure, including protected bike lanes and safe crossings

transit.why: Supports protecting frequency and reliability, expanding evening and night service where sensible, and fare gates paired with reduced and free fares.

evidence.quote: My second priority is protecting service: frequency, reliability, safety, and the rider experience.
Install modern, accessible fare gates at Link stations while expanding reduced and free fare programs for riders who qualify.

climate.summary: Mosqueda describes density and green housing as part of climate action and has highlighted salmon and watershed restoration grants as a Flood Control District supervisor. Duda said Metro's bus fleet electrification plan should be reassessed because of its cost. Duda's materials do not otherwise state climate positions.

strong_climate_action.why: Supports green housing and density as part of efforts to address climate change.

evidence.quote: promote density, greenspace, trees, and community cohesion as part of the effort to combat climate change

conservation.why: Highlighted Flood Control District grants for salmon recovery and watershed restoration in District 8.

evidence.quote: help create healthier communities, support salmon recovery, and ensure that environmental benefits are shared by current and future generations

energy_costs_first.why: Says Metro's fleet electrification plan should be reassessed because cost estimates were understated.

evidence.quote: Two specific areas that deserve reassessment are fleet electrification and fare collection.

schools.summary: Mosqueda lists expanding affordable child care as a priority. Duda's materials do not state a position on schools or child care funding.

child_care.why: Supports expanding affordable child care, including workforce pay and facilities.

evidence.quote: Expand accessible and affordable childcare in our county by supporting workforce pay, career pipelines and creating the infrastructure needed to deliver childcare service

health.summary: Both candidates support more behavioral health and addiction care. Mosqueda also calls for using county revenue tools to fund Harborview and public health clinics as federal Medicaid cuts take effect. Duda emphasizes stabilization centers, treatment capacity and fixing jail medical intake.

expand_coverage.why: Calls for using county revenue tools authorized by the state to fund Harborview and public health clinics as Medicaid coverage is cut.

evidence.quote: We have these revenue tools at our disposal to invest in the safety net that is Harborview and our public health clinics - the time to act is now.

behavioral_health.why: Supports more behavioral health services and the workers who provide them.

evidence.quote: invest in behavioral health
Increase access to care by investing in behavioral health services and workers

behavioral_health.why: Supports stabilization facilities for people in addiction or behavioral-health crises, and more residential treatment capacity.

evidence.quote: King County should develop stabilization facilities where law enforcement, outreach teams, and other responders can bring people experiencing serious addiction or behavioral-health crises.

economy.summary: Both candidates mention workforce training and apprenticeships. Mosqueda emphasizes worker protections, union jobs and Community Workforce Agreements, and support for small businesses. Duda proposes a plan to recruit advanced-manufacturing and other emerging industries with fast-tracked permits.

worker_protections.why: Supports worker protections, living-wage union jobs, apprenticeships and Community Workforce Agreements.

evidence.quote: good living wage union jobs through apprenticeships and Community Workforce Agreements
strengthen worker protections

small_business.why: Cites investments to support small businesses.

evidence.quote: I have delivered on policy and made significant investments to support small businesses

business_climate.why: Proposes a 'Frontier Industries' plan with a single point of contact and fast-tracked county permits for advanced manufacturing companies.

evidence.quote: Fast tracks qualifying advanced manufacturing projects, with measurable timelines
We should make King County the best place in America to build the technologies of the future

rights.summary: Mosqueda sponsored county measures restricting use of county property for civil immigration enforcement and pausing new detention facilities. Duda's materials do not state a position on immigration or civil rights policy.

protect_immigrants.why: Sponsored ordinances restricting county property from use in civil immigration enforcement and placing a moratorium on new detention facilities.

evidence.quote: the ordinance limits the use of county-owned and county-controlled property
the measure prohibits the county from accepting applications for new or expanded detention centers

government.summary: Both candidates say they support public services and accountability. Mosqueda emphasizes outcome benchmarks and oversight while opposing service cuts. Duda proposes public outcome statements for every program over $1 million a year, stronger audits, and shrinking or redesigning programs that repeatedly miss targets, and says the goal is better, not smaller, government.

transparency.why: Supports outcome benchmarks, transparent reporting and regular oversight hearings for contracted services.

evidence.quote: clear outcome benchmarks, transparent reporting, timely payments to contracted providers, and regular oversight hearings

public_services.why: Says both financial controls and social services investment are needed.

evidence.quote: Strong financial controls and robust social services investment are not mutually exclusive – we need both.

transparency.why: Supports public outcome statements, published results and stronger audits.

evidence.quote: Set measurable goals. Publish the results. Scale what works. Change what doesn't.
Require agencies to respond publicly to major audit findings.

public_services.why: Says he believes in robust public services that are measured for results.

evidence.quote: I believe in robust public services.

sos-1601668.background: Political and Partnerships Director at FairVote Washington and a Lake City resident; former PTA Advocacy Chair at John Rogers Elementary. She ran for District 5 in 2023 and applied for the 2025 council appointment; she has not held elected office, so there is no voting record.

sos-1601667.background: Director and faculty member at Seattle University and the University of Washington, co-founder and former chair of a community bank, and co-chair of the King County Immigrant and Refugee Commission. She applied for the 2025 council appointment; she has not held elected office, so there is no voting record.

housing.summary: Both candidates support building more housing and faster permitting, and both back Mayor Wilson's Taller Denser Faster direction. Jenks pledges 1,000 affordable units in the district, emphasizes public land, nonprofit partners and building next to light rail, and lists rental protections. Kang emphasizes shortening permit review, moving away from the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) fee framework in favor of JumpStart payroll-tax money for affordable housing, and pairing growth with infrastructure. On homelessness, Jenks stresses shelter, supportive housing and behavioral health response; Kang stresses on-demand addiction treatment and coordination of services.

build_more.why: Supports more housing near light rail and zoning and permitting changes to make affordable housing easier to build.

evidence.quote: We built the transit. We should let people live next to it. That is the heart of Taller Denser Faster
Faster has to actually mean faster. It cannot drift into 2028 while rents keep climbing

public_housing.why: Pledges 1,000 new affordable units in the district using public land and nonprofit developers; supports social housing.

evidence.quote: As a City Councilmember, Nilu Jenks will champion the creation of 1,000 new units of affordable housing in her district.
the City must use every tool available, public land, zoning flexibility, and partnerships with nonprofit developers
I really wanted the Fred Meyer's location that just went up in Lake City to get social housing

tenant_protections.why: Lists rental protections, along with shelter and affordable housing, as part of public safety.

evidence.quote: Nobody should be living on the street. It's enough shelter beds and it's enough affordable housing. It's rental protections

housing_first.why: Supports more shelter, supportive housing and affordable housing as the response to unsheltered homelessness.

evidence.quote: My biggest concern is our growing unsheltered homelessness crisis
We need more affordable housing, more supportive housing, and more housing overall.

build_more.why: Supports shortening permit review to build housing faster, and density with mixed-income housing.

evidence.quote: I’ll reduce permitting delays to build housing faster, support mixed-income and workforce housing near transit
Fixing our broken permitting system. That starts with shortening the permit review process
My focus is making sure we build smarter, not just faster

public_housing.why: Proposes directing more JumpStart payroll-tax revenue to affordable housing and continued investment in deeply affordable and supportive housing.

evidence.quote: Instead, we should direct more Payroll Expense Tax (“JumpStart”) revenue to fund affordable housing.
continued investment in deeply affordable and supportive housing so longtime residents aren't priced out

less_regulation_tax.why: Proposes moving away from the MHA fee on new housing and supported the proposed temporary MHA fee reduction.

evidence.quote: Moving away from the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) framework, which is a tax on desperately needed housing.
I am disappointed that Mayor Wilson chose not to move forward with the proposal

treatment.why: Supports expanding mental health and on-demand substance use treatment for unhoused people, alongside housing and coordinated services.

evidence.quote: My second priority is addressing chronic homelessness with care, treatment, housing, and accountability.
Expanding access to on-demand substance use disorder treatment so that our unhoused neighbors can get onto a path of recovery.

safety.summary: Both candidates support alternative responders through the CARE Department and gun violence prevention, and both said at a KUOW debate they would support a mini or satellite police precinct in North Seattle. Kang supports restoring police staffing, keeping SPD's CCTV cameras on along Aurora, and the SOAP (Stay Out of Areas of Prostitution) ordinance; she opposed cameras and SOAP early in the campaign and has said she changed her view after research. Jenks opposes the CCTV program and SOAP, emphasizes CARE, violence interruption, detectives and police oversight bodies, and has said she supports a 1,200-officer level. On guns, Jenks backs safe storage and violence intervention; Kang backs gun violence prevention and tracking how guns are owned and stored.

prevention.why: Supports a 24/7 CARE Department for behavioral health calls, community violence intervention and alternative response teams.

evidence.quote: It means a fully funded CARE Department responding 24/7 to behavioral health calls, working in true partnership with SPD and Fire Response so every call gets the right responder.
We should bring alternative response teams to fill this gap

more_police.why: Says she supports a 1,200-officer level and hiring detectives and undercover officers; has also said promises of large police hiring have not been met.

evidence.quote: I support 1,200 police. I've said actively, I support hiring detectives and undercover work that we saw was very successful on Aurora.
We haven’t hired 200 police officers, right? So people still offering the same solution.

tougher_enforcement.why: Opposes the SOAP ordinance and SPD's CCTV camera program on Aurora, citing results and civil-liberties concerns.

evidence.quote: We brought it back, it didn't work before, and it's not working now, so that's not maybe our best solution.
I strongly suggest people think about the trade-offs or civil liberties
I am very concerned about our cameras

police_accountability.why: Pledges to defend the independence of the city's police accountability bodies (CPC, OPA, OIG).

evidence.quote: She will also defend the independence of Seattle's police accountability bodies — the CPC, OPA, and OIG — so accountability has real teeth.

more_gun_laws.why: Supports safe storage efforts and community and hospital-based violence intervention.

evidence.quote: champion safe storage and school partnerships to keep guns out of young people's hands
Gun violence is a public health crisis, and Nilu will treat it like one.

more_police.why: Supports rebuilding SPD staffing and a second police precinct location in District 5.

evidence.quote: Building back Seattle Police Department staffing levels and moving forward with a second police precinct in District 5.
I fully support restoring the number of officers we need

tougher_enforcement.why: Supports the SOAP zone on Aurora, keeping SPD's CCTV cameras on with safeguards, and shutting down open-air drug markets; she opposed SOAP and cameras earlier in the race and says she changed her view after research.

evidence.quote: Using every tool in our tool box to bring pimps and johns to justice, including the Stay Out of Area Prostitution (SOAP) zone along Aurora Ave. N.
I also support we use the public safety cameras with ensuring that it is safe for all of the members and the rules we have such as SOAP.
I now believe the public safety benefits, particularly in addressing violent crime and improving investigations, outweigh the concerns that initially led me to oppose the technology.

prevention.why: Supports gun violence prevention and coordinating service providers, first responders, SPD and the CARE Department.

evidence.quote: coordinate providers, first responders, SPD, and CARE. I support police staffing, gun violence prevention, and enforcement focused on violent crime and trafficking.

more_gun_laws.why: Supports gun violence prevention and has said it is important to know who owns guns and how they are stored.

evidence.quote: I think it’s important for us to see who owns guns, how are they stored, and then all of those stolen and unmonitored, the guns that we can’t account for

cost.summary: Jenks says she is interested in progressive revenue and has proposed taxing AI use and data centers and a land value tax. Kang says the city should show a return on existing spending, has said she would not say more taxes are needed, and has criticized regressive sales tax increases, while also saying there are some opportunities to tax.

tax_wealthy.why: Supports progressive revenue, including taxing AI and requiring data centers to cover their costs.

evidence.quote: I am interested in progressive revenue, and so, that is basically shifting the burden
If we want data centers here, then we should be taxing them, they should be covering all the externalities

cut_spending.why: Says the city should review current spending and require a return on investments before adding taxes.

evidence.quote: We always make sure that every investment comes back with a return
We can’t just continue to tax, even though these are some opportunities to tax

no_new_taxes.why: Said at a forum that she would not say the city needs to collect more taxes from residents, and cites the burden of rising taxes.

evidence.quote: I wouldn’t say we need to collect more taxes from our constituents
The city must acknowledge the heavy financial burden it imposes on its own residents and local businesses through rising taxes, red tape, and inadequate basic services.

transport.summary: Both candidates prioritize completing North Seattle's missing sidewalks and better east-west transit connections in the district. Jenks also proposes expanding free transit to all students.

safe_streets.why: Makes sidewalk construction in District 5 a top priority.

evidence.quote: Nilu will make sidewalk construction a top priority, especially in District 5.
improve safety on Lake City Way and Aurora

transit.why: Proposes expanding free transit to all students, including college students.

evidence.quote: This includes expanding free child public transit to all students in Seattle, including college and university students.

safe_streets.why: Supports completing North Seattle's missing sidewalk network and improving walkability.

evidence.quote: Matching housing growth with basic public infrastructure like completing North Seattle’s missing sidewalk network and expanding transit access, especially for east to west connectivity.

transit.why: Wants added bus lines and better east-west transit access in the district.

evidence.quote: How can we not get rid of bus lines, but add to the bus lines, so we can all get there?

climate.summary: Jenks names meeting the city's climate goals as a priority and says JumpStart funds meant for the Green New Deal should not be used as a budget filler. Both candidates say tree canopy should be considered alongside new housing.

strong_climate_action.why: Lists meeting the city's climate goals as a priority and opposes using JumpStart Green New Deal money to fill budget gaps.

evidence.quote: move us toward meeting our climate goals
JumpStart funds were meant to support the Green New Deal, and we see it instead being a budget filler

conservation.why: Says tree canopy and biodiversity matter as the city adds density.

evidence.quote: That goes back to density, but with keeping in mind that tree canopy and biodiversity matters.

conservation.why: Supports protecting and expanding the urban tree canopy as housing grows.

evidence.quote: Protecting and expanding our urban tree canopy so that increased housing also means greener, healthier, and more climate-resilient neighborhoods.

schools.summary: Jenks proposes investing in affordable child care as part of a child-friendly city. Kang cites rising child care costs for families but has not stated a specific child care policy in the sources reviewed.

child_care.why: Supports investing in affordable child care.

evidence.quote: That means investing in affordable child care, improving walkability, increasing park safety, and designing public spaces with kids and families in mind

health.summary: Both candidates support expanding behavioral health and addiction services. Jenks emphasizes 24/7 CARE responses and upstream mental health investment; Kang emphasizes on-demand substance use disorder treatment.

behavioral_health.why: Supports investing in mental health and a 24/7 CARE response to behavioral health calls.

evidence.quote: That means investing upstream in housing, mental health, and youth so fewer crises happen in the first place.

behavioral_health.why: Supports expanding mental health and substance-use treatment, including on-demand treatment for unhoused people.

evidence.quote: I’ll expand mental health and substance-use treatment, connect people to housing and services
Expanding access to on-demand substance use disorder treatment so that our unhoused neighbors can get onto a path of recovery.

economy.summary: Both candidates say they will support neighborhood and immigrant-owned small businesses. Jenks has raised commercial rent stabilization; Kang has raised the cost of taxes, red tape and permitting on local businesses.

small_business.why: Lists supporting neighborhood businesses as a priority and has raised commercial rent stabilization.

evidence.quote: support neighborhood businesses
I'd be interested in commercial real estate stabilization.

small_business.why: Pledges support for immigrant-owned small businesses and cites the cost of taxes and red tape on local businesses.

evidence.quote: ensures that immigrant owned small businesses have the support they need to thrive

rights.summary: Both candidates support Seattle remaining a sanctuary city and limiting local involvement in federal immigration enforcement. Jenks, who works on ranked choice voting at FairVote Washington, makes implementing ranked choice voting in 2027 a priority; Kang serves on the King County election oversight committee but has not stated a position on ranked choice voting in the sources reviewed.

protect_immigrants.why: Supports sanctuary policies so local resources are not used for federal deportation efforts, and legal defense funds.

evidence.quote: Nilu will fight for robust sanctuary policies that ensure local resources are never used to support federal mass deportation efforts.

voting_access.why: Prioritizes successful implementation of ranked choice voting in 2027 and voter education.

evidence.quote: make sure ranked choice voting is successfully implemented in 2027 so voters trust and understand the system

protect_immigrants.why: Supports Seattle keeping its sanctuary city status and protecting workers of all visa statuses.

evidence.quote: Our city must maintain its status as a Sanctuary City and not allow federal immigration attacks to separate families or unjustly harm people living in our communities.

government.summary: Both candidates emphasize accountability and accessibility for District 5: Jenks proposes weekly drop-in office hours in the district, and Kang proposes district offices on Aurora and in Lake City and decisions guided by data and audits.

transparency.why: Calls for more accountable, responsive government and proposes weekly district office hours.

evidence.quote: The new District 5 councilmember must work every day to make government more accountable and responsive to neighbors’ needs

transparency.why: Says decisions should be guided by data and audits, and proposes district offices on Aurora and in Lake City.

evidence.quote: we need a leader who relies on data, audits, and lived experience to guide decisions, rather than pure ideology
I’m committed to setting up district offices on Aurora Ave and Lake City to increase accessibility to resources

sos-1601900.background: U.S. Representative for Washington's 7th District since 2017 and former Washington State Senator (2015-2017); founder and former executive director of the immigrant-advocacy group OneAmerica. Serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees.

record.text: Lead sponsor of H.R. 3069, the Medicare for All Act of 2025 (introduced April 29, 2025), to establish a national health insurance program.
Lead sponsor of H.R. 8085, the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2026 (introduced March 25, 2026), which would impose an annual tax on the net value of very large personal assets.
Lead sponsor of H.R. 4457, the Housing Is a Human Right Act of 2025 (introduced July 16, 2025), which authorizes federal grants for housing and homelessness programs.
Lead sponsor of H.R. 944, the Access to Counsel Act (2025), on access to legal counsel for people held at ports of entry or U.S. Customs and Border Protection facilities.
Voted No on final House passage of H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (motion to concur in the Senate amendment, roll call 190, July 3, 2025).
record.source: Clerk of the U.S. House, roll call vote

record.text: Voted Nay on H.R. 29, the Laken Riley Act, which requires federal detention of certain non-citizens charged with theft-related crimes (roll call 6, January 7, 2025).
record.source: Clerk of the U.S. House, roll call vote

sos-1601901.background: Business owner (Meineke franchises; former co-owner of Bistro Baffi restaurant in Normandy Park), U.S. Marine Corps veteran (2011-2014) and former Lakewood police officer (2017). Has not held elected office, so has no voting record.

housing.summary: Both candidates support federal money for housing. Jayapal sponsors the Housing Is a Human Right Act and lists housing and shelter funding she secured; Sheth says he will fight for federal funding to keep families in voucher-supported housing and calls for affordable housing to address homelessness.

public_housing.why: Sponsors the Housing Is a Human Right Act to fund affordable housing; lists federal housing funding secured for the district.

evidence.quote: the Housing is a Human Right Act to invest billions into affordable housing
$12.3 million for housing, including 300 new units and emergency shelter for 200 people

housing_first.why: Sponsors H.R. 4457, a federal bill on homelessness that funds housing and shelter programs, and cites emergency shelter funding.

evidence.quote: To address root causes of homelessness, meet the needs of community
build affordable housing

public_housing.why: Says he will seek federal funding to keep families in voucher-supported housing.

schools.summary: Stephens supports school choice, homeschooling support, and parental authority in education. No statement on these school priorities from Valdez was found beyond citing free school lunches as a use of new tax revenue.

parental_rights.why: Supports school choice and calls for respecting parental authority in education.

evidence.quote: We need to reduce bureaucracy in education, respect parental authority, and give all options – including homeschooling and charter alternatives – fair funding so every child can thrive.

health.summary: Valdez says he helped replace federal funding cut from Planned Parenthood. Stephens says health decisions belong to patients, families and doctors and emphasizes medical freedom; she did not state a position on the options listed here.

abortion_access.why: Says he helped backfill federal funding cut from Planned Parenthood.

evidence.quote: He also helped backfill money that Trump cut from Planned Parenthood

economy.summary: Valdez prime-sponsored a 2025 public employee collective bargaining law and cites tax relief for small businesses. No statement on these economic approaches from Stephens was found.

worker_protections.why: Prime sponsor of SSB 5503 (2025) on public employee collective bargaining, enacted.

evidence.quote: Concerning public employee collective bargaining processes.

small_business.why: Cites tax relief for small businesses and help for small, women- and minority-owned businesses.

evidence.quote: tax relief for small businesses
help working families, and small, women, and minority-owned businesses recover from the pandemic

rights.summary: Valdez names protecting immigrant communities as a top priority, describes applying an equity lens to policy, and has sponsored voter registration and ballot-curing bills. Stephens' rights page focuses on religious liberty and parental rights; no statement on the options listed here was found.

protect_immigrants.why: Lists fighting for immigrant communities as a top priority and cites limits on federal agents' masks and camera surveillance.

evidence.quote: continuing fighting for our immigrant and underserved communities
banned federal agents from using cameras to spy on immigrants

equity_programs.why: Says he brings a race and social justice equity lens to policy and budget decisions.

evidence.quote: I have worked tirelessly to bring a race and social justice equity lens to our policies and budget

voting_access.why: Prime sponsor of enacted bills expanding agency voter registration (SB 5077, 2025) and reducing ballot rejection rates (ESSB 5890, 2024).

evidence.quote: Concerning expansion of voter registration services by government agencies.
Reducing ballot rejection rates through updates to ballot curing, canvassing, reporting, and outreach processes.

government.summary: Stephens calls for audits of state spending and of nonprofits that receive public funds. No statement on these approaches to running government from Valdez was found.

transparency.why: Calls for full spending audits and accountability for taxpayer dollars, including funds passed to nonprofits.

evidence.quote: Before considering any new taxes, we need full audits of spending, aggressive cuts to waste and bureaucracy, and real accountability for how every taxpayer dollar is used.
